strengths: Addresses an important bottleneck in patch-token visual world-model planning: MPC rollouts with transformer latent states can be very expensive, and inference-time token sparsity is a natural and practically relevant direction.
The method is simple and easy to integrate with DINO-style patch-token world models: random token dropout during planning plus randomized grouped attention during training.
Evaluation covers a reasonably diverse set of simulated visual-control domains, including navigation, object pushing, deformable manipulation, and block pushing.

The paper reports both task success and planning-time tradeoffs, and includes useful ablations/comparisons against fixed masks, Latin hypercube sampling, attention-based pruning, LTRP, STAR, and clustering-based merging.
The empirical analyses using grouped-attention ablations, HSIC, probing, and noise robustness are helpful for understanding why random sparse rollouts can work.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. The core idea is essentially patch/token dropout for efficient transformer inference applied to DINO-WM-style planning; this is useful but feels incremental relative to existing ViT token pruning, PatchDropout, and world-model planning work.

The central efficiency claim is weakened by the reported runtimes: even sparse settings often take tens to hundreds of seconds per planning iteration, which does not convincingly support claims about real-time deployment. End-to-end latency per executed action, hardware details, batching assumptions, and wall-clock measurement protocol need clearer reporting.

The evaluation lacks statistical rigor. Success rates are reported over small numbers of episodes for some environments, with no confidence intervals or significance tests, despite many differences being within likely sampling noise. The apparent improvements over the full-patch baseline at some dropout rates may be noise or tuning effects.

Baselines are limited for a top-tier submission. The paper mainly compares against full-patch and CLS DINO-WM variants plus token-selection heuristics; it lacks comparisons to strong model-based RL/world-model methods, efficient transformer variants, distillation/compression methods, or task-specific policies where appropriate.

The method and fairness of comparisons need clarification. It is unclear whether the full-patch baseline uses the same grouped-attention training, whether grouped attention affects full-token performance, how positional encodings are handled after token dropping, and whether dropout ratios are selected post hoc per task.

Some technical claims are overstated or imprecise, such as saying computational cost scales exponentially with the number of tokens, whereas transformer attention is typically quadratic. The paper also claims adaptive adjustment, but the dropout ratio appears manually chosen rather than learned or adaptive.

The analysis is suggestive but not fully conclusive. HSIC/probing is performed mainly on Granular and uses coarse state summaries; the UMAP-based argument for Gaussian-like prediction error is weak; and the connection between these diagnostics and closed-loop control performance remains indirect.
All experiments are simulated, while the motivation emphasizes robotics and resource-constrained real-time applications. No real-robot or embedded-device evidence is provided.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant bottleneck in visual world-model planning: MPC rollouts over many ViT patch tokens are expensive, and reducing token count during imagination is a natural and practically motivated direction.
The proposed method is simple and easy to integrate into patch-token world models: randomized token dropout at planning time plus randomized grouped attention during training.
The empirical section covers several simulated visual control domains and reports both success rates and planning-time reductions, which is the right pair of metrics for the stated goal.

The paper includes useful ablations/comparisons against fixed random masks, Latin hypercube sampling, attention-based pruning, learned ranking, and clustering/merging approaches, supporting the claim that simple random dropout is competitive in this setup.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The core idea is essentially patch dropout/token subsampling applied to DINO-WM-style planning, with a randomized grouped-attention training trick. This feels incremental relative to existing ViT token reduction, patch dropout, and world-model planning work.

The evaluation is not strong enough for the main claims. Episode counts are small in several environments, especially 20-30 evaluations for deformable tasks, and the paper reports no confidence intervals, statistical tests, or seed variability for success rates. Several apparent improvements over the full-token baseline may be noise.

The baseline set is narrow for a top-tier submission. The main comparisons are full patches and CLS-token variants of DINO-WM, plus token selection heuristics. There is little comparison to broader efficient world-model, latent dynamics, recurrent state-space, or learned token-pruning methods trained end-to-end for this objective.

The claimed practical motivation of real-time or resource-constrained deployment is not convincingly supported. Reported planning times are extremely large, e.g. tens to hundreds of seconds per iteration, so even after speedups the method appears far from real-time control.

Some technical claims are overstated or imprecise. The paper says computational cost scales exponentially with the number of visual tokens, whereas transformer attention scales quadratically in token count. It also claims adaptive resource use, but the dropout ratio appears manually selected per setting rather than learned or automatically adapted.

The success-rate results are mixed. Performance degrades substantially at high dropout ratios, and on tasks such as PushT and Block Pushing the gains over full patches are inconsistent or marginal. The method requires task-dependent tuning of the dropout ratio, which weakens the generality claim.

The analysis sections are suggestive but not fully convincing. HSIC and attentive probing are only shown mainly on Granular-style state information and do not directly establish that the retained tokens are sufficient for planning across all tasks. The noise robustness argument relies on assumptions about dropout-induced prediction error that are only weakly validated.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives some implementation details, but does not clearly specify all environment/task success definitions, random seeds, variance over training runs, full hyperparameter selection procedure, or whether code/models will be released.

The writing has several clarity and polish issues, including awkward phrasing, typos, and occasional conceptual slippage, which makes parts of the methodology and experimental protocol harder to trust.

strengths: Clear and timely problem: reducing the computational cost of patch-token visual world models for MPC is important, especially as recent DINO-style world models become expensive during planning.
The proposed method is simple, practical, and well motivated: random token dropout plus randomized grouped attention is easy to implement and exposes a useful speed/accuracy knob at inference time.
Empirical coverage is fairly broad for this setting, with six visual control environments spanning navigation, pushing, deformable-object manipulation, and block manipulation.

The main results are promising: moderate dropout often preserves or improves success rates while reducing planning time substantially relative to full-patch planning, and consistently outperforms the CLS-token baseline on spatially demanding tasks.

The paper includes useful ablations and analyses, including grouped-attention training, dropout ratios, random versus fixed masks, comparisons to token selection/merging methods, HSIC/probing analysis, and noise robustness experiments.
The finding that simple random token sampling is competitive with more complex pruning or clustering methods is practically valuable and could influence future efficient world-model design.
weaknesses: The contribution is somewhat incremental conceptually: token dropout and sparse ViT inference are well-established, and the main novelty is their adaptation to world-model planning with a grouped-attention training scheme.
The evaluation is limited to simulated/offline benchmark settings; there is no real-robot or hardware-constrained deployment evidence despite claims about robotics and real-time applicability.

The reported planning times remain extremely large in absolute terms, often tens to hundreds of seconds per iteration, which weakens the paper's real-time deployment framing even if relative speedups are substantial.

The main comparisons are centered around full-patch and CLS-token DINO-WM-style baselines; stronger comparisons to other efficient world-model architectures, latent dynamics methods, or compute-matched alternatives would make the evidence more convincing.

Some evaluation settings have small sample sizes, especially Granular and Rope, and the paper reports limited statistical uncertainty for success rates, making it hard to judge whether several apparent improvements over the full-patch model are significant.

The claim that computational cost scales exponentially with the number of visual tokens is technically inaccurate for transformer attention, which is typically quadratic in token count; this should be corrected.
The dropout rate must be tuned per environment and the paper does not provide a principled selection rule or adaptive mechanism, limiting usability in new domains.
The method is tested primarily with DINO ViT-S/16 features, so generality to other encoders, token granularities, and larger or more modern world models remains uncertain.

strengths: The paper tackles an important practical bottleneck in visual world-model planning: transformer rollout cost during MPC. The proposed sparse imagination approach is simple, easy to implement, and directly targets the dominant self-attention cost.

The empirical scope is fairly broad, covering several simulated control domains, LIBERO-10, Meta-World, and small real-world LeRobot experiments. The paper reports both task success and planning-time reductions, which is appropriate for the claimed efficiency contribution.

The randomized grouped-attention training strategy is a plausible mechanism for making the world model robust to arbitrary token subsets, and the ablations indicate that it reduces prediction error and improves sparse-planning performance.

The comparison against several token-selection and merging alternatives is useful. The analysis of why random sampling can outperform static importance-based methods, especially the blind-spot argument, is an interesting and practically relevant observation.

The paper includes many implementation details and supplementary analyses, including timing breakdowns, encoder generalization, gradient-based planning, adaptive dropout, and prediction-quality measurements.
weaknesses: The core novelty is somewhat limited: random token dropout for transformer efficiency is conceptually simple and closely related to existing token pruning/dropout ideas. The paper’s main distinction is applying it to world-model imagination, which is useful but not deeply technically novel.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports. In particular, statements about applicability to complex real-world tasks and latest VLA systems rely on small-scale demonstrations, with real-world evaluation over only 10 trials per task and highly constrained setups.

The real-world evaluation is not fully convincing: PickPlace uses fixed cup position and held-out block positions, while Drawer appears to test on positions included in training. A manually selected goal image and goal proprioceptive state are used, which narrows the deployment claim.

Statistical treatment is weak. Most success rates are reported without confidence intervals or significance tests, despite small evaluation counts in several environments and differences that are often only a few percentage points.

The comparison to the full-patch baseline is sometimes hard to interpret because the sparse model uses a modified grouped-attention training procedure; it is not always clear whether performance differences reflect sparsification, training regularization, architecture differences, or evaluation variance.

The efficiency numbers are useful but somewhat surprising in absolute scale, with some planning iterations taking tens or hundreds of seconds. The paper would benefit from clearer hardware-normalized throughput, wall-clock deployment constraints, and a discussion of whether implementation overheads are representative.

The method is less plug-and-play than some wording suggests, since robust sparse inference appears to require retraining the world model with randomized grouped attention. This weakens the claim of seamless integration with arbitrary transformer world models.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone: although many hyperparameters are listed, code availability, pretrained models, exact evaluation seeds, and full training/evaluation protocols are not clearly provided.

strengths: The paper studies an important practical bottleneck: the high inference cost of token-rich visual world models during MPC-style planning.
The proposed random token dropout approach is simple, easy to implement, and appears to give meaningful wall-clock speedups in several settings.

The empirical section is broader than many robotics/world-model papers, covering several simulated domains, comparisons to CLS-token and token-selection alternatives, some architectural variants, and small real-robot demonstrations.
The paper includes useful ablations around grouped attention, sparsity levels, token-selection methods, and latency breakdowns, which help identify where the speedups come from.
weaknesses: The core novelty is limited. Random token dropout plus training-time masking/grouped attention is a straightforward adaptation of existing token sparsification/dropout ideas, and the paper does not convincingly establish a deeper technical contribution beyond applying this idea to visual world-model planning.

Several headline claims are stronger than the evidence. The paper claims broad applicability to complex real-world tasks and latest VLA systems, but the real-robot evaluation uses only two tasks, 10 trials each, fixed object/cup or drawer poses, a manually selected goal image and proprioceptive goal, and in one case tests on block positions included in training.

The evaluation has high variance and weak statistical support. Many results are based on 20-60 evaluations without confidence intervals or significance tests; some sparse variants outperform the full-token model in ways that may reflect noise rather than a robust advantage.

Performance preservation is inconsistent. At high drop ratios the method degrades sharply, and on tasks such as Block Pushing the absolute success rates are very low. The average numbers obscure substantial task-level failures.

The VLA-guided results are not very compelling: LIBERO improves only from 29% to 33%, matching full-patch planning but still at low absolute success; Meta-World gains are modest; and the comparison changes the original SmolVLA execution protocol by executing full action chunks, making positioning relative to prior work unclear.

The paper’s strongest baseline comparison is mostly against full-patch DINO-WM and CLS-token variants. It lacks comparison to alternative efficient planning strategies, smaller/faster world models, learned dynamic token selectors designed for control, adaptive compute baselines, or simply using the saved compute for more policy samples or replanning frequency.

The claim that random sampling is superior due to a fundamental blind-spot problem is only partially supported. The analysis is interesting, but the studied importance methods are largely static vision-token methods not necessarily designed for dynamic planning, so the conclusion may overgeneralize.

The method is presented as inference-time sparse imagination, but the reported robustness depends heavily on retraining the world model with randomized grouped attention. This weakens the claim of seamless integration with arbitrary transformer world models.

Planning-time numbers are hard to interpret. Some reported per-iteration times are extremely large, and the paper does not sufficiently normalize for hardware, implementation efficiency, batching, or alternative compute budgets.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite many details: there is no clear code release commitment, exact training/evaluation seeds and variance reporting are missing, and real-world data/protocol details are not sufficient to independently reproduce the strongest practical claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in visual world-model planning: quadratic token costs during repeated imagination rollouts. The proposed sparse imagination idea is simple, practical, and directly targets a real deployment constraint.

The experimental scope is broad and convincing for a systems-style contribution: navigation, rigid and deformable manipulation, LIBERO-10, Meta-World, and small-scale real-robot LeRobot tasks are all considered.

The core efficiency/performance tradeoff is well supported. Moderate token dropping often preserves full-patch planning performance while substantially reducing planning latency, and the paper reports both success rates and timing breakdowns.

The comparison against multiple token selection/merging alternatives is a notable strength. The analysis that static importance-based methods can create planning blind spots is interesting and helps explain why random sampling is competitive.
The randomized grouped attention training strategy is well motivated and ablated, with evidence that it improves sparse-token prediction and planning robustness.

The appendix provides many useful implementation details, hyperparameters, additional ablations, latency profiling, and probing analyses, which improves reproducibility relative to many robotics/world-model papers.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental: the main mechanism is random token dropout applied during world-model rollouts, combined with a training-time masking/grouping strategy. The paper’s strength is practical integration and evaluation rather than a deeply new algorithmic idea.

The real-world robot evidence is encouraging but limited. The evaluation uses only two tasks, fixed cup/drawer configurations, very small numbers of trials, and in one case test block positions include training positions, which weakens claims about robust real-world deployment.

Some headline claims feel stronger than the evidence. Phrases such as general applicability to complex real-world tasks and real-time robotic planning are only partially supported, since planning still adds overhead and the real-world setting is narrow.

The main baseline is full-patch DINO-WM plus CLS-token variants, with VLA-guided planning in later sections. It would be useful to compare more directly against other practical acceleration routes, such as lower-resolution encoders, smaller world models, learned latent bottlenecks, caching, or distillation.

Several reported gains in success rate are modest or within likely variance, especially for LIBERO-10 where VLA-only improves from 29% to 33%. Statistical confidence intervals or multiple seeds are not consistently reported for task success, making it hard to judge significance.

The adaptive dropout mechanism is preliminary and does not clearly improve over fixed ratios. Since the optimal dropout ratio is task-dependent, the lack of a mature adaptive policy limits usability in new domains.

The evaluation emphasizes matching the full-patch planner rather than improving absolute task performance. This is fair for an efficiency paper, but it also means the method inherits limitations of the underlying planner and world model, whose absolute performance is sometimes low, e.g. Block Pushing.
